18	The Defendants contend that the Complaint should be dismissed in its entirety for failure to comply with the 2004 Agreement’s dispute resolution and mediation clause. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. The clause provides that “[a]ny dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof shall first be referred by the parties to their senior-level executives for attempted resolution through good-faith negotiations.” Compl. Ex. A § 9.1 (emphasis added). Should negotiations fail, thirty days after making a written request to initiate those negotiations, “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require that the Dispute be referred to non-binding mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association.” Id. (emphasis added). The Defendants assert that Skold did not refer a dispute to a senior-level executive for negotiations and failed to make a written request that the dispute be referred to nonbinding mediation. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. Skold responds that the language of the mediation clause is permissive (“either Party may ... require”) and also argues that, in any event, Inc. has waived its right to invoke the clause because it participated in litigation over the dispute in the cancellation action before the TTAB. See Pl.’s L.P./Inc. Opp’n at 14-15.
19	The dispute resolution clause in the 2004 Agreement contains two clauses, one of which is mandatory (the parties shall refer the matter to senior executives to attempt to negotiate a resolution) and the other which is permissive (the parties may refer the matter to nonbinding mediation). Given the voluntary nature of the latter, this Court agrees with Skold that he was not required to refer this dispute to mediation before bringing suit here against Inc.
20	L.P. and S.A., who are not parties to the 2004 Agreement, also contend that the dispute resolution clause requires their dismissal from this action. In essence, they urge this Court to accept the contention that a nonparty to an agreement should be permitted to force a signatory party to engage in negotiations pursuant to a permissive mediation clause in that agreement as a condition precedent to filing suit but cite no relevant case or statute in support of this contention. See United States v. Benish, 5 F.3d 20, 26 (3d Cir.1993) (rejecting a party’s claim where the party “provided] no legal support for his argument or any persuasive reason” for the court to find in his favor). The Court sees no persuasive reason to dismiss Skold’s entire Complaint based on this unsupported argument. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss the Complaint against L.P. and S.A. on this ground shall be denied.
21	Regarding Inc.: although Skold did fail to bring in a senior-level executive to try to resolve the dispute — as he was required to do under the dispute resolution provision — Inc.’s participation in the TTAB proceedings waived any rights it may have had to seek to have the parties’ executives negotiate an end to the dispute. See, e.g., LBL Skysystems (USA), Inc. v. APG-Am., Inc., No. 02-5379, 2005 WL 2140240, at *30 (E.D.Pa. Aug. 31, 2005) (holding that a “party that engages in discovery and files pretrial motions waives a contract’s alternative dispute resolution provision”); Smith v. IMG Worldwide, Inc., 360 F.Supp.2d 681, 687 (E.D.Pa.2005) (finding that a party’s engaging in motion practice and providing “substantial discovery” constituted waiver of contractual alternative dispute resolution provision).
22	Viewing the four years’ worth of docket entries in the TTAB action, the Court considers that Inc. did not file a motion to stay the TTAB proceedings pending executive-level negotiations and instead filed, inter alia, motions to dismiss, a protective order, multiple summary judgment motions (one of which was partially granted in its favor), and a final brief in preparation for trial. See, e.g., Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897, 2012 WL 5902083 (T.T.A.B. Nov. 8, 2012) (granting Inc.’s motion for partial summary judgment on Skold’s abandonment claim). See also generally Registrant’s Trial Brief, Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897 (T.T.A.B. Aug. 13, 2014), Docket No. 81. This four-year history of litigation in the cancellation action — from filing nearly through trial — is, on its face, inconsistent with the notion that Inc. was willing to engage in the good-faith executive-level negotiations required by the dispute resolution provision.
23	Moreover, the Court can look to the TTAB’s grant of partial summary judgment in favor of Inc. and dismissing Skold’s abandonment claim as a concrete example of an instance where Inc.’s conduct inconsistent with the dispute resolution clause caused prejudice to Skold, not to mention the expenditure of time, cost, and resources attendant to maintaining a multi-year trademark cancellation action. The Defendants have undisputedly accepted the judicial process and have demonstrated that fact by: (1) Inc.’s failure to raise the issue of good-faith negotiations promptly before the TTAB; (2) Inc.’s engaging in discovery in the TTAB action; (3) Inc.’s filing of several pretrial motions in the TTAB action, none of which raise the issue of negotiation; and (4) the Defendants’ decision to wait until the case was ready to proceed to trial before the TTAB and until a Complaint was filed in this Court before asserting Skold’s failure to negotiate as grounds for a motion to dismiss. See St. Clair Area Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. E.I. Assocs., 733 A.2d 677, 682 n. 6 (Pa.Commw.Ct.1999) (“The key to determining whether [an alternative dispute resolution procedure] has been waived is whether the party, by virtue of its conduct, has accepted the judicial process.”). Inc. cannot now attempt to stand on the alternative dispute resolution clause as a reason for dismissal. Its right to invoke the clause has been waived.
24	```

12	International ACH and Wire Transactions If your Account receives incoming ACH transactions (either credits or debits) or wire transfers initiated from outside of the United States, both you and we are subject to the Operating Rules and Guidelines of the National Automated Clearing House Association (“NACHA”) or the rules of any wire transfer system involved, and the laws enforced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”). Under such rules and laws, we may temporarily suspend processing of a transaction for greater scrutiny or verification against the OFAC list of blocked parties, which may result in delayed settlement, posting and/or availability of funds. If we determine there is a violation, or if we cannot satisfactorily resolve a suspected or potential violation, the subject funds will be blocked as required by law. If you believe you have adequate grounds to seek the return of any blocked funds, it is your sole responsibility to pursue the matter with the appropriate governmental authorities. Please see the OFAC website for procedures and form required to seek a release of blocked funds.

18	The bulk of Plaintiffs’ breach claim centers around their argument that TD’s conduct violated the NACHA Rules, which Plaintiffs claim were incorporated into the Account Agreement. See Compl. at ¶ 166-67. In order to address this claim we must first determine whether the NACHA rules were in fact incorporated. 154	    "name": "Definition — \"Cash Sweep Mechanism\"",
155	    "text": "\"Cash Sweep Mechanism\" means: (i) for the First Sweep Period, on each Sweep Payment Date for each Sweep Date occurring in such period, if the Reference Cash Sweep DSCR for the Sweep Date immediately preceding such Sweep Payment Date results in an amount in excess of 1.25, the Lenders and the Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors shall have the right to receive an aggregate amount (a \"First Sweep Period Sweep Amount\") equal to fifty percent (50%) of (x) Reference Cash Sweep DSCR minus 1.25, multiplied by (y) the amount of Reference Cash Sweep Debt Service; (ii) for the Second Sweep Period, on each Sweep Payment Date for each Sweep Date occurring in such period, if the Reference Cash Sweep DSCR for the Sweep Date immediately preceding such Sweep Payment Date results in an amount (a \"Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount\") in excess of 1.15, the Lenders and the Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors shall have the right to receive an aggregate amount equal to fifty percent (50%) of (x) Reference Cash Sweep DSCR minus 1.15, multiplied by (y) the amount of Reference Cash Sweep Debt Service; (iii) the Lenders and Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors shall have the right to receive on each Sweep Payment Date the Sweep Amount for such Sweep Payment Date, first out of cash available in the Escrow Account for such payment, and then, to the extent of any deficiency in cash available in the Escrow Account on a Sweep Payment Date to fully pay the Sweep Amount, out of cash in the DSRA. In this definition: \"First Sweep Period\" means the period commencing on the date that is nine (9) months following the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date, to but excluding April 1, 2014. \"Reference Cash Sweep DSCR\" means for any Sweep Date the actual Cash Sweep DSCR determined as at the last day of, and for, the fiscal quarter immediately preceding such Sweep Date. \"Reference Cash Sweep Debt Service\" means for any Sweep Date the actual Cash Sweep Debt Service determined as at the last day of, and for, the fiscal quarter immediately preceding such Sweep Date. Credit Agreement -7- \"Sweep Amount\" means a First Sweep Period Sweep Amount or a Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount. \"Second Sweep Period\" means the period commencing on and including April l, 2014 to and including the Term Loan Maturity Date. \"Sweep Date\" means each date that is one (1) Business Day following the last day of each full fiscal quarter during the applicable Sweep Period, including the fourth fiscal quarter. \"Sweep Payment Date\" means each date that is one (1) Business Day following the last day of the fiscal quarter, including the fourth fiscal quarter, in which a Sweep Date occurs (that is, for example, if the Sweep Date occurs on April l for the preceding fiscal quarter ending March 31, the Sweep Payment Date for such Sweep Date shall be July 1 or the first Business Day thereafter if July 1 is not a Business Day). \"Sweep Period\" means the First Sweep Period or the Second Sweep Period, as the case may be."

{"clause_id":"c209","reasoning_cat1":"\"Other institutional lender\" is a mild catch-all after two specifics, and the parenthetical \"(other than the Borrower)\" is redundant.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with \"Working Capital Bank Financing\", though the instrument uses three different labels for that financing.","prob_cat1":0.11,"prob_cat2":0.14},

{"clause_id":"c211","reasoning_cat1":"A conventional interpretation clause; \"unless the context requires otherwise\" is a familiar and workable qualifier.","reasoning_cat2":"It equates \"will\" with \"shall\" and makes \"including\" non-exhaustive, which magnifies the catch-alls elsewhere, but it does not contradict any provision.","prob_cat1":0.12,"prob_cat2":0.10},
{"clause_id":"c212","reasoning_cat1":"A long provision with reciprocal notice mechanics and a closing sentence — \"all of the financial calculations, computations and definitions hereunder shall not include any double counting\" — that states a result without a method.","reasoning_cat2":"That anti-double-counting sentence is doing real work reconciling overlapping definitions such as Long-Term Debt, Short-Term Debt, Total Debt and the two Net Finance Charges measures; and it imposes IFRS for Guarantors against a GAAP definition drawn \"with respect to any Person\".","prob_cat1":0.23,"prob_cat2":0.22},
{"clause_id":"c213","reasoning_cat1":"Clear on availability and non-reborrowing, though the proviso mixing requested loans with loans \"arising by the automatic conversion of an LC Disbursement\" packs two different mechanics into one test.","reasoning_cat2":"It says the undrawn commitment \"shall lapse automatically\" at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period, yet Section 2.06 contemplates letters of credit outstanding and converting into Term Loans well after that date; those two cannot both operate literally.","prob_cat1":0.21,"prob_cat2":0.36},
{"clause_id":"c214","reasoning_cat1":"Sub-facility caps and conditions are stated with figures and section references; readable.","reasoning_cat2":"Section 2.02(b) also makes any unborrowed Tranche A amount available under Tranche B, so Tranche A-2 and Tranche B overlap on the same money; a court could be asked which conditions apply.","prob_cat1":0.13,"prob_cat2":0.25},
{"clause_id":"c215","reasoning_cat1":"The parenthetical importing \"any remaining amount of the Initial Lender Tranche A Total Commitment to the extent not previously borrowed\" makes the Tranche B cap indeterminate on its face.","reasoning_cat2":"The same unborrowed Tranche A amount is already available under Section 2.02(a)(ii) on Section 4.02 conditions, but here it becomes available on the different Section 4.03 conditions; the two routes to the same money are not reconciled.","prob_cat1":0.21,"prob_cat2":0.28},
{"clause_id":"c216","reasoning_cat1":"A short deferral to the Accession Agreement.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with \"Accession Project Financing\", \"Term Loan Commitment\" and the Total Commitment cap.","prob_cat1":0.07,"prob_cat2":0.11},
{"clause_id":"c217","reasoning_cat1":"\"The payment of the Project's costs and Transaction Costs amounts\" is garbled, and neither category is bounded, so what proceeds may fund is loose.","reasoning_cat2":"The prohibition on using proceeds to fund the DSRA sits beside Section 2.06(j), which requires cash collateral to be deposited in the DSRA following an Event of Default, and Section 5.15's Required Amount; the funding sources for that account are scattered.","prob_cat1":0.25,"prob_cat2":0.23},
{"clause_id":"c218","reasoning_cat1":"Clear discretion for the Borrower subject to a commitment cap; the parenthetical \"(including with respect to its LC Exposure)\" is compressed but usable.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with Section 2.01's Unused Commitment test and Section 2.06(a); the non-ratable borrowing right sits oddly with Section 2.09's \"ratable account of the Lenders\" repayment but they address different things.","prob_cat1":0.12,"prob_cat2":0.17},
{"clause_id":"c219","reasoning_cat1":"A standard several-liability provision, clearly expressed.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with Section 2.03(a)'s non-ratable borrowing and Section 2.18's pro rata sharing; no conflict found in the supplied text.","prob_cat1":0.06,"prob_cat2":0.08},
{"clause_id":"c220","reasoning_cat1":"\"Each Borrowing shall be comprised entirely of Eurodollar Rate Borrowings\" is circular — a Borrowing composed of Borrowings — and the defined term is itself framed as a question of \"whether\".","reasoning_cat2":"\"Borrowing\" includes an LC Exposure, which cannot sensibly bear a Eurodollar rate, and Section 2.06(h) prices unconverted LC Disbursements by a separate three-month LIBO formula; the general rule and the LC mechanics do not mesh.","prob_cat1":0.30,"prob_cat2":0.27},
{"clause_id":"c221","reasoning_cat1":"\"In an amount of not less than ten million Dollars ... in not more than fifteen (15) Borrowings\" fuses a size floor and a count cap in one clause without saying what the fifteen applies to — per lender, per tranche, or overall.","reasoning_cat2":"The proviso disapplies both limits for LC conversions and lets an Accession Agreement vary them, which is consistent, but the count cap interacts with Section 2.03(a)'s freedom to draw from different lenders.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.19},
{"clause_id":"c222","reasoning_cat1":"The opening is garbled (\"shall notify the Facility Agent and the Escrow Agent and Account Bank of such request and in writing not later than 1:00 p.m.\"), and the passage saying Lenders \"may\" fund under Section 2.14 \"but they shall have no obligation to do so\" makes the commitment illusory in that state.","reasoning_cat2":"It requires the initial Interest Period to be specified here while Section 2.07(b) says the election is made in the first Borrowing Request and the \"Interest Election Request\" definition treats it as a separate one-time request; three provisions describe one act.","prob_cat1":0.28,"prob_cat2":0.27},
{"clause_id":"c223","reasoning_cat1":"Clear funding mechanics, with a consequential-damages waiver that is plainly worded.","reasoning_cat2":"Funds go to the Escrow Account, which under its own definition exists to receive all Cash for application under the Cash Sweep Mechanism, yet here the Escrow Agent must make the funds available to the Borrower for its stated purposes; the account's two functions pull in different directions.","prob_cat1":0.14,"prob_cat2":0.29},
{"clause_id":"c224","reasoning_cat1":"A dense, doubled sentence repeating the same Unused Commitment test twice, with an embedded proviso for undrawn expired letters of credit; hard to follow but each limb is stated.","reasoning_cat2":"The June 30, 2013 issuance cut-off, the four-year expiry limit and the September 30, 2013 end of the Term Loan Availability Period do not line up, since LC Disbursements convert into Term Loans against commitments that will have lapsed.","prob_cat1":0.26,"prob_cat2":0.30},
{"clause_id":"c225","reasoning_cat1":"The documentary conditions are set out as alternatives (i)-(v) closing with \"(vi) such other documents as may be specified by the Issuing Bank from time to time\" — an open catch-all after specifics, layered with \"reasonably acceptable in form and substance to the Issuing Bank\".","reasoning_cat2":"The deemed representation about LC Exposure repeats the Section 2.06(a) cap, and the reference to submitting the Issuing Bank Agreement matches Exhibit C; consistent.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.16},
{"clause_id":"c226","reasoning_cat1":"A short, definite two-limb expiry rule.","reasoning_cat2":"The \"Letter of Credit\" definition adds a fourth condition allowing negotiation until December 30, 2014, a day after four years from the December 29, 2010 date of this Agreement; the two outer limits do not agree.","prob_cat1":0.09,"prob_cat2":0.31},
{"clause_id":"c227","reasoning_cat1":"The conversion timing rules are stated twice with overlapping five-Business-Day conditions and a \"succeeding Business Day that is five (5) Business Days after\" formula that is hard to apply to a given disbursement.","reasoning_cat2":"Conversion creates Term Loans that must fit within an Unused Commitment which Section 2.01 says lapses at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period, and Section 2.09 amortises only loans outstanding on that date; the conversion machinery outlives both.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.31},
{"clause_id":"c228","reasoning_cat1":"A long but conventional obligations-absolute clause with an express carve-back for direct damages from failure to exercise care; carefully drafted.","reasoning_cat2":"That carve-back is in tension with Section 2.06(g), which says the Issuing Bank has \"the final word\" and the Borrower \"will not question its decision\" absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud.","prob_cat1":0.17,"prob_cat2":0.31},
{"clause_id":"c229","reasoning_cat1":"\"The Issuing Bank will have the final word ... and the Borrower will not question its decision\" is colloquial, one-sided drafting whose effect on the Borrower's remedies is genuinely arguable.","reasoning_cat2":"Section 2.06(f) expressly preserves the Issuing Bank's liability for direct damages caused by a failure to exercise care in examining documents, a lower threshold than the gross negligence/wilful misconduct/fraud standard imposed here.","prob_cat1":0.34,"prob_cat2":0.40},
{"clause_id":"c230","reasoning_cat1":"A definite interest formula keyed to a three-month LIBO Rate plus the Interest Margin.","reasoning_cat2":"It presupposes a gap between disbursement and conversion that Section 2.06(e) says will normally be nil or five Business Days, and it prices at three months regardless of the Interest Period elected under Section 2.07.","prob_cat1":0.13,"prob_cat2":0.19},
{"clause_id":"c231","reasoning_cat1":"The trigger sentence stacks acceleration and automatic bankruptcy defaults awkwardly, but the obligation and the return mechanic are stated clearly.","reasoning_cat2":"Cash collateral is deposited into the DSRA \"as supplemental to the Required Amount\", while Section 2.02(d) prohibits funding the DSRA with Loan proceeds and Section 5.15 sets the Required Amount; the account serves two purposes at once.","prob_cat1":0.19,"prob_cat2":0.26},
{"clause_id":"c232","reasoning_cat1":"The enumeration runs \"(i) ... and (iii)\" with no clause (ii), the same mechanical gap that appears in the \"Interest Period\" definition.","reasoning_cat2":"It reproduces the \"Interest Period\" definition almost verbatim, so the defect is duplicated rather than resolved, and Section 2.07(b) makes the election part of the Borrowing Request rather than a separate request as the definition of \"Interest Election Request\" supposes.","prob_cat1":0.39,"prob_cat2":0.29},
{"clause_id":"c233","reasoning_cat1":"Two short, definite sentences.","reasoning_cat2":"It equates the Interest Election Request with the first Borrowing Request, whereas the defined term treats it as a separate \"one-time request ... in accordance with Section 2.07\"; a modest labelling inconsistency.","prob_cat1":0.10,"prob_cat2":0.21},
{"clause_id":"c234","reasoning_cat1":"A plain notification duty.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with Sections 2.04 and 2.07(a)-(b); no conflict found.","prob_cat1":0.07,"prob_cat2":0.09},
{"clause_id":"c235","reasoning_cat1":"A short conditional deferral to Section 2.13(c).","reasoning_cat2":"Section 2.13 is not reproduced, but the default-interest hook is consistent with Article VII references elsewhere.","prob_cat1":0.06,"prob_cat2":0.10},
{"clause_id":"c236","reasoning_cat1":"The provision requires \"prior written notice to the Borrower\" and cancellation \"immediately upon such notice\", then says the Lenders \"shall endeavor to provide prior notice\" except where creditworthiness has deteriorated — an internal contradiction about whether notice is mandatory; \"for any reason, including\" also makes the enumerated grounds pure surplusage.","reasoning_cat2":"An unfettered right to cancel Unused Commitments at will sits uneasily with Section 2.02's availability promises and Section 2.06(a)'s letter-of-credit facility, which depend on Unused Commitment continuing to exist.","prob_cat1":0.43,"prob_cat2":0.32},
{"clause_id":"c237","reasoning_cat1":"The reduction right is conditioned on Project costs being \"reduced below one billion ninety seven million Dollars\", a figure with no operative source in the body of the agreement.","reasoning_cat2":"That number appears only in the recitals, and there only as what the total cost \"is currently estimated to be\" — using an estimate in a recital as an operative trigger is the classic recital-versus-operative problem.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.36},
{"clause_id":"c238","reasoning_cat1":"The text says \"twenty-three (23) approximately equal installments\" then sets out a twenty-four-row table, and the Business Day convention (\"next preceding Business Day\") cuts against the extension convention used for Interest Periods.","reasoning_cat2":"It amortises only \"all Term Loans outstanding on the last day of the Term Loan Availability Period\", yet LC Disbursements can convert into Term Loans long after that date, and the final installment falls on January 1, 2020, which will not be a Business Day though the proviso requires payment on the Term Loan Maturity Date.","prob_cat1":0.29,"prob_cat2":0.32},
{"clause_id":"c239","reasoning_cat1":"A short, standard record-keeping obligation.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with Section 2.10(b) and the evidence-of-debt scheme.","prob_cat1":0.05,"prob_cat2":0.06},
{"clause_id":"c240","reasoning_cat1":"The provision breaks off mid-sentence after \"the Interest Period applicable\", so as reproduced it states an obligation without completing its content.","reasoning_cat2":"It parallels Section 2.10(a)'s lender accounts and would ordinarily be followed by a prima facie evidence sentence; nothing in the supplied text contradicts it.","prob_cat1":0.24,"prob_cat2":0.10}
]}
